# Flask

> A small Python web framework: one application object that turns WSGI requests into calls to your view functions and turns their return values back into HTTP responses.

**701/701 citations verified** against the code at `85c5d93c` on 2026-11-06. Generated by [Onramp](https://github.com/SanyamWadhwa07/onramp).

Flask is the Pallets project's WSGI web framework, here at version `3.2.0.dev` [`pyproject.toml:1-4`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L1-L4). You create one `Flask` object, register view functions on it with decorators, and hand that object to a WSGI server; the server calls it once per HTTP request [`src/flask/app.py:1529-1536`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1529-L1536). Flask itself is mostly glue: HTTP parsing and routing come from Werkzeug, templates from Jinja, cookie signing from ItsDangerous, the CLI from Click and signals from Blinker [`pyproject.toml:23-30`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L23-L30). This guide is for someone who wants to understand, change or maintain the framework itself, not just use it.

*In one picture:* Flask is like a restaurant's front desk with a recipe binder. During setup you file recipes (view functions) under dish names (endpoints) and pin house rules to the wall (hooks, error handlers, config). During service, each order (request) gets its own ticket clipped to the counter (the request context), the desk looks up the recipe, runs the house rules before and after, and hands back the plate (the response). The analogy stops working at one point: the 'ticket on the counter' is not passed to the cook; any code can glance at the counter (the `request` proxy) and see the ticket for the order it is serving right now.

## The gist

### What Flask is: one object a web server calls

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** Flask is a WSGI framework: you build one `Flask` object, register functions on it, and a web server calls that object once per request. Almost everything else is borrowed from Werkzeug and Jinja.

A web server such as gunicorn knows nothing about your code. It speaks WSGI, a small Python contract: for every request it calls one object as `app(environ, start_response)`. In Flask that object is your `Flask` instance; its `__call__` hands straight to `wsgi_app` [`src/flask/app.py:1529-1536`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1529-L1536).

What you write is setup. The README's whole example is five lines [`README.md:22-31`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/README.md#L22-L31). `@app.route("/")` files `hello` under the endpoint name `hello` and adds a URL rule for `/`. When a request for `/` arrives, Flask matches the rule, calls `hello()`, and turns the returned string into an HTTP response.

Flask is small because it delegates. Six packages do the heavy lifting [`pyproject.toml:23-30`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L23-L30): Werkzeug parses HTTP and routes URLs, Jinja renders templates, ItsDangerous signs the session cookie, Click builds the `flask` command, Blinker sends signals and MarkupSafe marks safe HTML. Flask's own job is the glue: deciding when each piece runs and giving you one object to configure.

The design notes also say what is left out on purpose: Flask will never have a database layer or a form library [`docs/design.rst:206-213`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/design.rst#L206-L213). Extensions fill those gaps and keep their state in `app.extensions` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:379-388`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L379-L388).

The code you will read is about 9,200 lines in `src/flask`, a third of them docstrings, plus a large test suite in `tests/` and three example apps in `examples/`.

> **Checkpoint:** A WSGI server receives a request for your app. What does it call?
> - Your view function `hello()` directly
> - The `Flask` object, as `app(environ, start_response)`
> - The `flask run` command, which forwards the request
> - Werkzeug's router, which then imports your module
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The `Flask` object, as `app(environ, start_response)`. The server only knows the WSGI contract, so it calls the app object, whose `__call__` forwards to `wsgi_app` [`src/flask/app.py:1529-1536`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1529-L1536). Your view is called much later, by `dispatch_request`.</details>

### The mental model: setup fills registries, serving reads them

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** A Flask app lives in two phases: setup, where decorators fill registries on the app object, and serving, where each request reads them. Flask refuses most setup calls once serving has started.

Hold this picture and most of the code falls into place.

**Setup** is all the code outside your view functions: `Flask(__name__)`, loading config, `@app.route`, `@app.before_request`, `app.register_blueprint(...)`. Each of those calls only writes into a dict or list on the app. `before_request`, for example, is a single append to `before_request_funcs[None]` [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:483-484`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L483-L484). Routes go into `url_map` and `view_functions` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:650-661`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L650-L661).

**Serving** starts with the first request. `full_dispatch_request` sets `_got_first_request = True` [`src/flask/app.py:911`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L911) and from then on only reads the registries: which before-hooks to run, which view matches, which error handler applies.

Why a hard line? A production server runs your app in several worker processes. A route added inside one worker during a request would exist only in that worker, so the docs require all setup to finish before serving [`docs/lifecycle.rst:36-48`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/lifecycle.rst#L36-L48). Flask enforces part of this: registration methods are wrapped in `@setupmethod`, which calls `_check_setup_finished` first [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:42-49`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L42-L49). On the app that raises `AssertionError` once a request has been handled [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:413-423`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L413-L423); on a blueprint, once it has been registered.

Two habits follow from this and appear everywhere: an app factory (`create_app()`) does all setup in one function, and tests build a fresh app for each test. The tutorial's factory is a clean example [`examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py:6-51`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py#L6-L51).

> **Checkpoint:** A view function calls `app.add_url_rule('/new', ...)` while handling a request. What happens?
> - The route is added for every worker
> - Flask raises AssertionError because setup is finished
> - The route is queued until the next restart
> - Werkzeug ignores it silently
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Flask raises AssertionError because setup is finished. `add_url_rule` is a `@setupmethod`; `_check_setup_finished` raises once `_got_first_request` is true [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:413-423`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L413-L423).</details>

## Run it

### Set up a development checkout

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** Install with `uv sync`, run `uv run pytest`, and you have a working checkout. Every tool is configured in `pyproject.toml`.

You need Python 3.10 or newer [`pyproject.toml:22`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L22). The repository is locked with `uv.lock`, and `pyproject.toml` declares dependency groups instead of requirement files: `tests`, `typing`, `docs`, `dev` and a few more. `uv sync` installs Flask in editable mode plus the default groups `dev`, `pre-commit`, `tests` and `typing` [`pyproject.toml:104-105`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L104-L105).

Then run `uv run pytest`. Two settings matter: tests are collected from `tests/`, and every warning becomes an error [`pyproject.toml:107-111`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L107-L111). A `DeprecationWarning` from a dependency fails the run instead of scrolling past. That is deliberate: Flask deprecates and removes APIs on a schedule, and the suite should notice early.

Without uv, a plain venv works: `pip install -e .` plus the `tests` group, which is `asgiref`, `greenlet`, `pytest` and `python-dotenv` [`pyproject.toml:58-63`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L58-L63). If `asgiref` is missing, the async tests are skipped rather than failing [`tests/test_async.py:11`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/test_async.py#L11).

The same file configures tox environments for each Python version, minimum and development dependency versions, style, typing and docs [`pyproject.toml:171-179`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L171-L179). CI runs those environments through uv on Linux, Windows and macOS [`.github/workflows/tests.yaml:15-34`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/.github/workflows/tests.yaml#L15-L34).

The environment variables in the panel below (`FLASK_APP`, `FLASK_DEBUG` and friends) only matter when you run an app; you do not need them to work on Flask itself.

> **Checkpoint:** A new test fails only on CI's 'Development Versions' job, with a DeprecationWarning from Werkzeug's main branch. Why does a warning fail the test?
> - CI uses a different pytest plugin
> - pytest is configured with `filterwarnings = error` in pyproject.toml
> - tox treats any stderr output as a failure
> - The leak detector fixture fails on warnings
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>pytest is configured with `filterwarnings = error` in pyproject.toml. Warnings are turned into errors for the whole suite [`pyproject.toml:107-111`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L107-L111), and the dev job installs unreleased Pallets libraries that may deprecate things early [`pyproject.toml:214-231`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L214-L231).</details>

### Run an app: `flask run` and the tutorial blog

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** `flask --app <module> run --debug` finds your app, turns on the reloader and debugger, and serves on 127.0.0.1:5000. The tutorial in examples/tutorial is the best real app to run first.

Save the README example as `app.py` and run `flask run`. With no `--app` option and no `FLASK_APP` variable, the CLI tries to import `wsgi.py` and then `app.py` from the current folder [`src/flask/cli.py:351-356`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L351-L356). Inside the module it looks for an object called `app` or `application`, then for the only `Flask` instance, then for a `create_app` or `make_app` factory [`src/flask/cli.py:41-91`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L41-L91).

`--debug` writes `FLASK_DEBUG=1` into the environment before the app is imported [`src/flask/cli.py:479-481`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L479-L481), which turns on the auto-reloader and the in-browser debugger [`src/flask/cli.py:973-979`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L973-L979). The defaults are host 127.0.0.1 and port 5000 [`src/flask/cli.py:883-884`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L883-L884).

For something real, run the tutorial blog, `flaskr`: `flask --app flaskr init-db` creates the SQLite schema, then `flask --app flaskr run --debug` [`examples/tutorial/README.rst:48-53`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/examples/tutorial/README.rst#L48-L53). Read its files in this order: `__init__.py` (the factory), `db.py` (a connection per request on `g`), `auth.py` (sessions and login), `blog.py` (the CRUD views). Between them they use almost every public feature: instance-folder config, blueprints, `before_app_request`, `teardown_appcontext`, `flash`, `abort`, `url_for` and a custom CLI command.

One trap: an `app.run()` call at the bottom of a module. Under `flask run` it is ignored with a red warning, because the CLI sets `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI` [`src/flask/app.py:609-621`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L609-L621). Put `app.run()` behind `if __name__ == "__main__":` if you want both ways to work.

### How Flask's own tests and CI are set up

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Flask's tests use a fresh `app` fixture with `TESTING=True`, reset `FLASK_*` environment variables around every test, and fail if a request context leaks. CI runs the suite on three operating systems, PyPy, and minimum and development dependency versions.

Open `tests/conftest.py` before writing a test. The `app` fixture builds `Flask("flask_test", root_path=...)` with `TESTING=True` and a secret key [`tests/conftest.py:44-51`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/conftest.py#L44-L51); `client`, `app_ctx` and `req_ctx` build on it. Two autouse fixtures guard every test. One removes `FLASK_APP`, `FLASK_DEBUG`, `FLASK_RUN_FROM_CLI` and similar variables and restores them afterwards [`tests/conftest.py:11-41`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/conftest.py#L11-L41), because the CLI writes to `os.environ`. The other, `leak_detector`, pops any request context still pushed after the test and fails if it found one [`tests/conftest.py:84-95`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/conftest.py#L84-L95).

`TESTING=True` matters more than it looks. With `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` left at `None`, an unhandled error is re-raised into the test instead of becoming a 500 page [`src/flask/app.py:841-852`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L841-L852), so you see the real traceback.

The CLI tests import tiny apps from `tests/test_apps`, which the `test_apps` fixture puts on `sys.path` [`tests/conftest.py:71-81`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/conftest.py#L71-L81). Type checking is part of quality control too: mypy runs in strict mode over `src` and `tests/type_check` [`pyproject.toml:127-132`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L127-L132).

CI runs tox through uv for Python 3.10 to 3.13, on Windows and macOS, on PyPy, with the minimum version of every dependency and with the development branches of the Pallets libraries [`.github/workflows/tests.yaml:15-34`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/.github/workflows/tests.yaml#L15-L34). If a change works locally but fails 'Minimum Versions', you used a Werkzeug or Click feature newer than the floor pinned in `tests-min` [`pyproject.toml:195-212`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L195-L212).

> **Checkpoint:** A new test calls `app.test_request_context().push()` and never pops it. What happens?
> - Nothing; contexts are garbage-collected
> - The autouse `leak_detector` fixture pops it and fails the test
> - The next test silently reuses the context
> - pytest prints a warning, which is ignored
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The autouse `leak_detector` fixture pops it and fails the test. `leak_detector` runs after every test, pops leaked request contexts and asserts the list is empty [`tests/conftest.py:84-95`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/conftest.py#L84-L95).</details>

## The stack

### Primer: WSGI, the contract Flask implements

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** WSGI is the contract between a Python web server and an app: the server calls `app(environ, start_response)` and iterates over what it returns. `Flask.wsgi_app` is that function.

WSGI (the Web Server Gateway Interface, PEP 3333) has three parts. The server turns an HTTP request into a dict called `environ`: `REQUEST_METHOD`, `PATH_INFO`, `QUERY_STRING`, headers as `HTTP_*` keys, `wsgi.input` for the body and `wsgi.errors` for log output. It calls your application with that dict and a callback, `start_response(status, headers)`. The application calls `start_response` once and returns an iterable of bytes, which the server writes to the socket.

Flask's docs list the round trip in eight steps [`docs/lifecycle.rst:78-87`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/lifecycle.rst#L78-L87). In code, `Flask.wsgi_app` is exactly that function: build a context from `environ`, compute a response, return `response(environ, start_response)` [`src/flask/app.py:1479-1527`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1479-L1527). The last call works because a Werkzeug `Response` is itself a small WSGI app.

Middleware is a WSGI app that wraps another one. Flask asks you to wrap `app.wsgi_app` rather than `app`, so the `Flask` object stays reachable [`src/flask/app.py:1483-1490`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1483-L1490). A common example is Werkzeug's `ProxyFix`, which corrects the environ when the app runs behind a reverse proxy [`docs/lifecycle.rst:104-107`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/lifecycle.rst#L104-L107).

Two consequences. Your app is just an object, so any WSGI server can host it and the test client can call it without a network. And WSGI is synchronous: one call per request, one worker busy until it returns. That is why async views still tie up a worker [`docs/async-await.rst:36-45`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/async-await.rst#L36-L45).

> **Checkpoint:** You want middleware that logs every request path, and you still want `app.config` to work afterwards. Where do you install it?
> - `app = LoggingMiddleware(app)`
> - `app.wsgi_app = LoggingMiddleware(app.wsgi_app)`
> - Inside a view function
> - Inside `start_response`
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>`app.wsgi_app = LoggingMiddleware(app.wsgi_app)`. Replacing `app` would hide the Flask object behind the middleware; the docstring recommends wrapping `wsgi_app` instead [`src/flask/app.py:1483-1493`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1483-L1493).</details>

### Primer: what Werkzeug provides

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Werkzeug supplies Flask's request and response objects, the URL router, HTTP exceptions, `LocalProxy`, the test client and the development server. Flask mostly subclasses and configures them.

Most of what feels like Flask at the HTTP level is Werkzeug. Four pieces matter when you read the code.

**Request and Response.** `flask.Request` subclasses Werkzeug's request and adds routing results and config-backed limits [`src/flask/wrappers.py:18-57`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/wrappers.py#L18-L57); `flask.Response` changes the default mimetype to `text/html` [`src/flask/wrappers.py:222-244`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/wrappers.py#L222-L244). Form parsing, cookies, headers and `.get_json()` are inherited.

**Routing.** A `Map` holds `Rule`s; each rule has a pattern like `/<int:id>/update`, allowed methods and an endpoint name. Flask creates the map from `url_map_class` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:405`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L405) and each rule from `url_rule_class` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:650-653`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L650-L653). Binding the map to one request gives a `MapAdapter`: `match()` finds the rule and URL variables, `build()` does the reverse for `url_for` [`src/flask/app.py:1109-1116`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1109-L1116). Werkzeug orders rules by complexity, so registration order does not matter [`docs/design.rst:80-93`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/design.rst#L80-L93).

**HTTP exceptions.** `NotFound`, `MethodNotAllowed`, `BadRequest` and the rest are exceptions that are also responses. `abort(404)` raises one; a routing failure is stored on `request.routing_exception` and raised later [`src/flask/app.py:889-891`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L889-L891).

**Utilities.** `LocalProxy` powers `request` and `g` [`src/flask/globals.py:6`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/globals.py#L6); `werkzeug.test.Client` is the base of `FlaskClient`; `run_simple` is the dev server behind `flask run` [`src/flask/cli.py:983-993`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L983-L993).

When Flask calls a method you cannot find in `src/flask`, it is almost always inherited from Werkzeug, whose minimum supported version is 3.1.0 [`pyproject.toml:29`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L29).

### Primer: Jinja and how Flask configures it

*standard · 4 min*

**In short:** Jinja renders templates. Flask creates one Jinja environment per app with a loader that searches the app and its blueprints, and autoescaping for HTML-like files.

A Jinja template is text with holes: `{{ post.title }}` prints a value, `{% for post in posts %}` loops, `{% extends "base.html" %}` inherits a layout. Jinja compiles each template to Python once and renders it with a dict of variables.

The settings live in an `Environment`. Flask builds its own the first time something touches `app.jinja_env`, and caches it [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:469-477`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L469-L477). `create_jinja_environment` turns on autoescaping through `select_jinja_autoescape`, sets `auto_reload` from `TEMPLATES_AUTO_RELOAD` or debug mode, and adds globals: `url_for`, `get_flashed_messages`, `config`, `request`, `session` and `g` [`src/flask/app.py:385-423`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L385-L423).

Autoescaping applies to names ending in `.html`, `.htm`, `.xml`, `.xhtml` and `.svg` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:536-547`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L536-L547), so `{{ user_input }}` cannot inject markup in those files. In other files, or once you use `|safe` or `Markup`, it does not protect you.

Flask's `Environment` subclass changes one thing: the default loader is `DispatchingJinjaLoader` [`src/flask/templating.py:39-49`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L39-L49), which tries the app's `templates/` folder and then each blueprint's folder in registration order. The first match wins, so an app template overrides a blueprint template with the same name.

Because the environment is created lazily and cached, `app.jinja_options` must be set before the first render; later changes have no effect [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:242-251`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L242-L251).

### Primer: Click, Blinker and ItsDangerous

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Three small libraries do three narrow jobs: Click builds the `flask` command, Blinker broadcasts signals, ItsDangerous signs the session cookie.

**Click** turns decorated functions into a command-line program. `@click.command()` makes a command, `@click.option(...)` adds an option, and a `click.Group` holds subcommands. The `flask` program is a `FlaskGroup` instance named `cli` [`src/flask/cli.py:1110-1119`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L1110-L1119), and every app gets its own `AppGroup` so you can write `@app.cli.command()` [`src/flask/app.py:252-260`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L252-L260). `AppGroup.command` wraps your function so it always runs inside an app context [`src/flask/cli.py:413-427`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L413-L427).

**Blinker** is publish/subscribe. Flask defines ten signals in a private namespace [`src/flask/signals.py:1-17`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/signals.py#L1-L17) and calls `.send(app, ...)` at fixed points, such as `request_started` at the top of `full_dispatch_request` [`src/flask/app.py:914`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L914). Receivers observe; they cannot change the outcome.

**ItsDangerous** signs data with a secret key. The session interface builds a `URLSafeTimedSerializer` from `SECRET_KEY` (plus `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`), the salt `cookie-session`, HMAC and SHA-1 [`src/flask/sessions.py:303-335`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sessions.py#L303-L335). `dumps` produces the data plus a timestamp and a signature; `loads(val, max_age=...)` raises `BadSignature` if either was changed or the value is too old [`src/flask/sessions.py:344-349`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sessions.py#L344-L349). The data is encoded, not encrypted.

Two optional packages complete the picture: `asgiref` for async views and `python-dotenv` for `.env` files, installed as the `async` and `dotenv` extras [`pyproject.toml:32-34`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L32-L34). The table below lists every technology with where it is used.

## The map

### The map: one class hierarchy and a ring of helpers

*core · 6 min*

**In short:** Flask is one class hierarchy (`Scaffold` → `App` → `Flask`) plus a ring of single-purpose modules: contexts and proxies, request/response wrappers, sessions, templating, JSON, blueprints, the CLI and the test client.

Start with the class hierarchy, because almost every method you look for lives on one of three classes. `Scaffold` holds what apps and blueprints share: the route decorators and the hook registries [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:52-68`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L52-L68). `App` adds what only an app has, such as `config`, `url_map`, `blueprints` and error-handler lookup [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:59`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L59). `Flask` adds the parts that do I/O: `wsgi_app`, dispatching, response building, contexts and the Jinja environment [`src/flask/app.py:81`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L81). Blueprints mirror this: `Scaffold` → sans-IO `Blueprint` → `flask.Blueprint`.

Around the hierarchy sit single-purpose modules:
- `ctx.py` and `globals.py`: the two contexts and the proxies `current_app`, `g`, `request`, `session`.
- `wrappers.py`: `Request` and `Response`.
- `sessions.py` and `json/tag.py`: the signed-cookie session.
- `templating.py`: the Jinja environment, loader and `render_template`.
- `json/`: the `app.json` provider and `jsonify`.
- `helpers.py`: `url_for`, `redirect`, `abort`, `flash`, `send_file`.
- `cli.py` and `testing.py`: two more ways to drive the same app.
- `config.py`, `signals.py`, `typing.py`: leaves that import nothing else from Flask.

The app points at its collaborators through class attributes, which is how you customize Flask without monkeypatching: `request_class`, `response_class` and `session_interface` [`src/flask/app.py:212-224`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L212-L224), then `config_class`, `app_ctx_globals_class`, `json_provider_class`, `url_rule_class`, `url_map_class` and `test_client_class` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:185-269`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L185-L269). Set one on a subclass and every request uses it.

The diagram below shows who calls whom during a request.

> **Checkpoint:** You want every request to use a custom Request subclass with an extra property. What is the intended way?
> - Monkeypatch `werkzeug.wrappers.Request`
> - Set `request_class` on a Flask subclass or on the app
> - Wrap `request` in a new LocalProxy
> - Override `RequestContext.push`
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Set `request_class` on a Flask subclass or on the app. The request context builds the request from that attribute [`src/flask/ctx.py:317-319`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L317-L319).</details>

### Two halves: the sans-IO core and the I/O layer

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** Since 3.0, the parts of `Flask` and `Blueprint` that do no I/O live in `src/flask/sansio/`, so Quart can reuse them. When you look for a method, check both halves.

In June 2023 commit `0ec7f713`, released in Flask 3.0 [`CHANGES.rst:100-101`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/CHANGES.rst#L100-L101), split the app and blueprint classes in two so that 'async based IO projects, specifically Quart' can base themselves on Flask. The rule for the new folder is short: no I/O, nothing on a likely I/O path, no Flask globals [`src/flask/sansio/README.md:1-6`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/README.md#L1-L6).

What ended up where:
- `sansio/scaffold.py`: `Scaffold`, the decorators and registries, `setupmethod`, `find_package`.
- `sansio/app.py`: `App`, with config creation, `add_url_rule`, template filter registration, `register_blueprint`, `_find_error_handler`, `trap_http_exception`, `redirect` and `inject_url_defaults`.
- `sansio/blueprints.py`: `Blueprint` and `BlueprintSetupState`, which is all of blueprint registration.
- `app.py`: `Flask(App)`, everything that touches `request`, `request_ctx` or a WSGI environ.
- `blueprints.py`: `Blueprint(SansioBlueprint)`, adding a Click group and static-file serving.

You can see the seams. `App.create_jinja_environment` only raises `NotImplementedError` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:479-480`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L479-L480), and `Scaffold.add_url_rule` is a documented stub [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:367-433`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L367-L433) that `App` and `Blueprint` override. The type aliases bend for Quart too: `ResponseValue` accepts async iterables 'for Quart, until App is generic' [`src/flask/typing.py:11-23`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/typing.py#L11-L23).

The cost is duplication. `Flask` and `flask.Blueprint` both define `get_send_file_max_age` and `send_static_file`, with a note saying so [`src/flask/blueprints.py:55-65`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/blueprints.py#L55-L65), and the long class docstring appears in both `app.py` and `sansio/app.py`. When you fix one copy, grep for the other.

> **Checkpoint:** You want to change how `add_url_rule` picks default HTTP methods. Which file do you edit?
> - src/flask/app.py
> - src/flask/sansio/app.py
> - src/flask/blueprints.py
> - src/flask/wrappers.py
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>src/flask/sansio/app.py. The real `add_url_rule` is on the sans-IO `App` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:616-628`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L616-L628); blueprints end up calling it too.</details>

### Folder tour: package, tests, examples, docs

*standard · 4 min*

**In short:** Four top-level folders matter: `src/flask` (the package), `tests` (the suite and tiny test apps), `examples` (three runnable apps) and `docs` (Sphinx docs that double as design notes).

- `src/flask/`: 24 Python modules, about 9,200 lines. The `src` layout (since 2019, commit `ca278a86`) is the usual way to make tests import the installed package rather than the source folder by accident.
- `src/flask/sansio/`: the I/O-free base classes.
- `src/flask/json/`: the JSON provider, `jsonify`, and the tagged serializer used by sessions.
- `tests/`: about 370 test functions; `test_basic.py` alone has 93. `tests/test_apps/` holds small importable apps for the CLI tests, such as `cliapp/factory.py` [`tests/test_apps/cliapp/factory.py:4-13`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/tests/test_apps/cliapp/factory.py#L4-L13), and `tests/type_check/` holds files that exist only to be type-checked [`pyproject.toml:127-130`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L127-L130).
- `examples/tutorial/`: the `flaskr` blog from the official tutorial, with its own tests.
- `examples/javascript/`: one JSON endpoint called from fetch, XHR and jQuery pages [`examples/javascript/js_example/views.py:8-18`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/examples/javascript/js_example/views.py#L8-L18).
- `examples/celery/`: running Celery tasks inside an app context.
- `docs/`: the documentation. `lifecycle.rst`, `design.rst`, `appcontext.rst` and `reqcontext.rst` are the most useful for understanding the code; `CHANGES.rst` at the root is the changelog.
- The root: `pyproject.toml` (all tool config), `uv.lock`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (ruff and file hygiene hooks), `.github/workflows/` (CI) and `.devcontainer/`.

There is no `requirements/` folder any more and no `setup.py`: packaging is flit, configured in `pyproject.toml` [`pyproject.toml:85-90`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/pyproject.toml#L85-L90). The language breakdown below comes from the scanner.

## Core ideas

### Registries keyed by scope

*core · 5 min*

**In short:** Every decorator on an app or blueprint writes into a dict keyed by scope: `None` for the whole app, a blueprint name for that blueprint. At request time Flask reads those dicts for the scopes of the current request.

Open `Scaffold.__init__` and you have Flask's whole registration model [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:102-215`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L102-L215). There are eight structures:
- `view_functions`: endpoint name → function.
- `error_handler_spec`: scope → status code → exception class → handler [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:110-126`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L110-L126).
- `before_request_funcs`, `after_request_funcs`, `teardown_request_funcs`: scope → list of functions.
- `template_context_processors`: scope → list, preloaded with the default processor under `None` [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:182-184`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L182-L184).
- `url_value_preprocessors`, `url_default_functions`: scope → list.

The scope key is typed `str | None` [`src/flask/typing.py:49`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/typing.py#L49). `None` means every request; a string is the registered name of a blueprint, such as `auth` or `parent.child`.

Decorators are thin. `@app.before_request` appends to `before_request_funcs[None]` and returns the function unchanged [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:459-484`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L459-L484). On a blueprint the same decorator fills the blueprint's own dict under `None`; at registration `_merge_blueprint_funcs` copies it into the app under the blueprint's name [`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:379-410`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py#L379-L410).

At request time Flask builds the list of scopes from the request: `None` plus `request.blueprints`, the current blueprint and its parents. `preprocess_request` walks the app first, then outer to inner blueprints [`src/flask/app.py:1281-1294`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1281-L1294); `process_response` walks the innermost blueprint first and the app last, each list reversed [`src/flask/app.py:1316-1319`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1316-L1319).

That one pattern explains why a blueprint's `before_request` does not run for app routes, why `before_app_request` exists, and why after-hooks run in reverse.

> **Checkpoint:** Blueprint `admin` registers `@bp.before_request`. A request hits an app-level route `/`. Does the function run?
> - Yes, before_request functions run for every request
> - No; it is filed under the scope 'admin', and `/` belongs to no blueprint
> - Only if the blueprint was registered first
> - Only in debug mode
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>No; it is filed under the scope 'admin', and `/` belongs to no blueprint. For `/`, `request.blueprints` is empty, so only the `None` scope is walked [`src/flask/wrappers.py:180-195`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/wrappers.py#L180-L195). Use `before_app_request` to run for every request.</details>

### Routes, rules and endpoints

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** `@app.route` becomes a Werkzeug `Rule` in `app.url_map` plus an entry in `app.view_functions`. The endpoint name links the two, defaults to the function name, and is what `url_for` builds from.

`route` is a decorator factory: it pops `endpoint` from the options and calls `add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, f, **options)` [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:360-363`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L360-L363). `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete` and `patch` are shortcuts that set `methods` for you [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:284-301`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L284-L301).

`App.add_url_rule` does the real work [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:604-661`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L604-L661):
1. The endpoint defaults to `view_func.__name__`.
2. Methods default to the view's own `methods` attribute, else `("GET",)`. A plain string such as `methods="POST"` is rejected with a `TypeError`.
3. Unless the view or the `PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS` setting says otherwise, `OPTIONS` is added and answered automatically. `HEAD` is added for `GET` routes too [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:352-353`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L352-L353).
4. A `Rule` is created and added to `url_map`.
5. The function is stored in `view_functions[endpoint]`; a different function for an existing endpoint raises `AssertionError`.

The endpoint is the join key. At dispatch the matched rule's endpoint picks the function [`src/flask/app.py:902`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L902). For URLs, `url_for('blog.update', id=3)` asks the bound adapter to build that endpoint. Inside a request it builds a path; outside one it needs `SERVER_NAME` and builds an absolute URL, or raises a `RuntimeError` saying what to configure [`src/flask/app.py:1079-1100`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1079-L1100). An endpoint starting with `.` is relative to the current blueprint [`src/flask/app.py:1066-1072`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1066-L1072).

Blueprints prefix both: rule `/login` becomes `/auth/login`, endpoint `login` becomes `auth.login`. The tutorial even adds a rule with no view, `add_url_rule("/", endpoint="index")`, so `url_for('index')` builds `/` while the blog blueprint's `index` view serves it [`examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py:45-49`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/examples/tutorial/flaskr/__init__.py#L45-L49).

> **Checkpoint:** `url_for('index')` raises RuntimeError inside a background script. What is the most likely fix?
> - Register the route again
> - Configure SERVER_NAME (plus APPLICATION_ROOT and PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME as needed) and run inside an app context
> - Move the route into a blueprint
> - Call `app.run()` first
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>Configure SERVER_NAME (plus APPLICATION_ROOT and PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME as needed) and run inside an app context. Outside a request the adapter comes from `create_url_adapter(None)`, which needs `SERVER_NAME` [`src/flask/app.py:468-476`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L468-L476); without it `url_for` raises the error [`src/flask/app.py:1089-1095`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1089-L1095).</details>

### Contexts and the proxies `request`, `session`, `g`, `current_app`

*core · 8 min*

**In short:** `current_app`, `g`, `request` and `session` are proxies that look up the current context every time you use them. An app context makes the first two work; a request context makes the last two work and pushes an app context for you.

Your view never receives the request as an argument, yet `request.form` works. The trick is two pieces of storage that are private to the current thread or async task, Python `ContextVar`s declared in `globals.py`: `_cv_app` and `_cv_request` [`src/flask/globals.py:24-42`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/globals.py#L24-L42). On top of them sit Werkzeug `LocalProxy` objects. `request` is `LocalProxy(_cv_request, "request")`, so every attribute access becomes `_cv_request.get().request.<attr>` at that moment [`src/flask/globals.py:46-48`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/globals.py#L46-L48). If nothing is set, the proxy raises `RuntimeError` with the familiar 'Working outside of request context' text [`src/flask/globals.py:35-41`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/globals.py#L35-L41).

What gets stored are two small objects from `ctx.py`:
- `AppContext` holds `app`, a URL adapter and a fresh `g` [`src/flask/ctx.py:245-249`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L245-L249). `current_app` and `g` read from it.
- `RequestContext` holds `app`, the `Request` built from the environ, the URL adapter, the session and the flashed messages [`src/flask/ctx.py:309-335`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L309-L335). `request` and `session` read from it.

Pushing sets the ContextVar and keeps the returned token; popping resets with that token, which restores whatever was there before, so contexts nest cleanly. `RequestContext.push` first makes sure an app context for the same app is active and pushes one if not [`src/flask/ctx.py:370-378`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L370-L378). That is why `current_app` and `g` work in views.

Who pushes contexts? `wsgi_app` for every request, the CLI for app commands, `app.test_request_context()` and `app.app_context()` when you ask, and `stream_with_context` while a streamed response runs. Background work needs its own app context, as the Celery example shows [`examples/celery/src/task_app/__init__.py:29-39`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/examples/celery/src/task_app/__init__.py#L29-L39).

To test for a context in code, `has_request_context()` and `has_app_context()` simply check whether the ContextVar is set [`src/flask/ctx.py:225-235`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L225-L235).

<details><summary>Go deeper</summary>

Where the state lives matters for nesting. If an app context for the same app is already active, `RequestContext.push` reuses it and records `None` instead of an app context to pop [`src/flask/ctx.py:370-376`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L370-L376). So inside `with app.app_context():` every test-client request shares your `g`. Outside it, each request gets a new app context and a new `g`. The full push/pop sequence is traced in the 'How `request` and `g` become available' flow.

</details>

> **Checkpoint:** In a view you start a `threading.Thread` whose function reads `request.args`. It raises RuntimeError. Why?
> - `request` only works in the main thread of the process
> - A new thread starts with an empty context, so `_cv_request` is not set there
> - Threads cannot import flask
> - The request was already garbage-collected
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>A new thread starts with an empty context, so `_cv_request` is not set there. The proxies read ContextVars, and in standard CPython a new thread does not inherit the caller's values. Push a context in the thread or pass the data in; `copy_current_request_context` exists for greenlets [`src/flask/ctx.py:155-193`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L155-L193).</details>

### How a return value becomes a Response

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** A view may return a string, bytes, a dict or list, a generator, a Response, a WSGI callable, or a tuple adding status and headers. `Flask.make_response` turns all of them into one `Response`.

`make_response` [`src/flask/app.py:1129-1137`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1129-L1137) works in three passes.

**Unpack tuples.** A 3-tuple is `(body, status, headers)`. A 2-tuple is `(body, headers)` if the second item is a `Headers`, dict, tuple or list, otherwise `(body, status)`. Any other length is a `TypeError` [`src/flask/app.py:1190-1208`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1190-L1208).

**Convert the body.** `None` is an error whose message names the endpoint, because a forgotten `return` is a common bug [`src/flask/app.py:1211-1216`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1211-L1216). Then:
- `str`, `bytes`, `bytearray` or any iterator → `response_class(body, status=..., headers=...)` [`src/flask/app.py:1219-1229`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1219-L1229). A generator becomes a streamed response.
- `dict` or `list` → `self.json.response(body)`, the app's JSON provider [`src/flask/app.py:1230-1231`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1230-L1231).
- another Werkzeug response class, or any callable → `response_class.force_type(body, environ)`, which runs a WSGI callable if needed.
- anything else → a `TypeError` listing the allowed types.

**Apply status and headers.** A string status like `"201 CREATED"` sets `status`; an integer sets `status_code`. Headers are added with `update`, so they extend rather than replace [`src/flask/app.py:1258-1267`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1258-L1267).

The same function handles error-handler results and `before_request` short-circuits, because `finalize_request` calls it on whatever produced the value [`src/flask/app.py:939`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L939). `flask.make_response(...)` in your own code calls it too, giving you a real `Response` to add headers to [`src/flask/helpers.py:181-185`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/helpers.py#L181-L185). The type checker knows these rules as `ResponseReturnValue` [`src/flask/typing.py:35-42`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/typing.py#L35-L42).

> **Checkpoint:** A view returns `({'ok': True}, 201, {'X-Id': '7'})`. What does the client get?
> - A TypeError: dicts cannot be inside tuples
> - A JSON response with status 201 and the X-Id header
> - An HTML page showing the dict
> - A 200 response; status is ignored for JSON
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>A JSON response with status 201 and the X-Id header. The 3-tuple is unpacked, the dict goes through `self.json.response`, then status and headers are applied [`src/flask/app.py:1258-1267`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1258-L1267).</details>

### Error handlers and the 500 fallback

*standard · 6 min*

**In short:** Exceptions from hooks and views go to `handle_user_exception`, which finds a handler by status code and exception class. Anything unhandled reaches `handle_exception`, which re-raises in debug or testing mode and otherwise returns a logged 500.

**Registration.** `@app.errorhandler(404)` or `@app.errorhandler(DatabaseError)` calls `register_error_handler`, which normalizes the argument: `404` becomes `(NotFound, 404)`, a custom exception becomes `(DatabaseError, None)`, and an instance or non-exception is rejected [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:641-698`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L641-L698). The handler is stored at `error_handler_spec[None][code][cls]`.

**Lookup.** `_find_error_handler` tries the blueprint handler for the code, the app handler for the code, the blueprint handler for the class, then the app handler for the class. For classes it walks the exception's MRO, so a handler for `HTTPException` catches every HTTP error without a more specific handler [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:823-846`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L823-L846).

**The path an exception takes:**
1. `full_dispatch_request` catches any `Exception` and calls `handle_user_exception` [`src/flask/app.py:779-809`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L779-L809).
2. HTTP exceptions go to `handle_http_exception`, which returns the exception itself (it is a valid response) if no handler exists. Routing redirects pass through untouched [`src/flask/app.py:763-777`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L763-L777).
3. Other exceptions with no handler are re-raised.
4. In `wsgi_app`, a re-raised exception reaches `handle_exception` [`src/flask/app.py:811-862`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L811-L862). It sends `got_request_exception`. If `PROPAGATE_EXCEPTIONS` is true, or unset while testing or debugging, it re-raises so you see the traceback. Otherwise it logs the error and builds an `InternalServerError` with `original_exception` set, passing it to a 500 handler if one exists.

Two settings change step 2. `TRAP_HTTP_EXCEPTIONS` treats HTTP errors like ordinary exceptions; `TRAP_BAD_REQUEST_ERRORS`, on by default in debug mode for `BadRequestKeyError`, makes a missing form key show a traceback instead of a bare 400 [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:848-881`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L848-L881).

> **Checkpoint:** An app has `@app.errorhandler(500)`, testing and debug are off, and a view raises `KeyError`. What does the handler receive?
> - The KeyError
> - An InternalServerError whose `original_exception` is the KeyError
> - None
> - Nothing; the handler is not called for non-HTTP errors
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>An InternalServerError whose `original_exception` is the KeyError. `handle_exception` always passes an `InternalServerError` to the 500 handler [`src/flask/app.py:855-860`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L855-L860).</details>

### Rendering templates and context processors

*standard · 5 min*

**In short:** `render_template` asks the app's Jinja environment for the template, runs context processors to add `g`, `request`, `session` and your own values, sends two signals, and renders.

`render_template(name, **context)` is three lines: get the real app object, ask `app.jinja_env.get_or_select_template` (a list of names means 'the first that exists'), and call `_render` [`src/flask/templating.py:138-150`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L138-L150). `_render` does the interesting part [`src/flask/templating.py:126-135`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L126-L135):
1. `app.update_template_context(context)` runs the app's context processors (`None` scope), then each blueprint's for the current request, outermost first. It keeps a copy of your arguments and re-applies it at the end, so values you pass explicitly always win [`src/flask/app.py:506-532`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L506-L532).
2. `before_render_template` is sent.
3. Jinja renders.
4. `template_rendered` is sent; tests use it to capture which template rendered with which context.

The default context processor adds `g`, and inside a request `request` and `session` [`src/flask/templating.py:24-36`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L24-L36). They are also environment globals, so imported macros can see them [`src/flask/app.py:411-421`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L411-L421).

Finding the file is the loader's job. `DispatchingJinjaLoader` tries the app's `templates/` folder first, then every blueprint's folder in registration order [`src/flask/templating.py:91-109`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L91-L109). A blueprint's `template_folder` is `None` unless you set it, so it has no loader by default [`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:271-282`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py#L271-L282). If the wrong template seems to load, set `EXPLAIN_TEMPLATE_LOADING = True`; every attempt is logged with the loader's details [`src/flask/debughelpers.py:124-178`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/debughelpers.py#L124-L178).

`stream_template` is the generator version. It wraps the generator in `stream_with_context` when a request is active, so `request` still works while the response streams [`src/flask/templating.py:165-185`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L165-L185).

> **Checkpoint:** Both `templates/index.html` in the app and `templates/index.html` in a blueprint exist. A blueprint view calls `render_template('index.html')`. Which file renders?
> - The blueprint's, because the view belongs to the blueprint
> - The app's, because the app's loader is tried first
> - Whichever file changed last
> - Neither; TemplateNotFound is raised for ambiguity
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>The app's, because the app's loader is tried first. The loader yields the app's loader before any blueprint's, and the first match wins [`src/flask/templating.py:101-109`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L101-L109). Put blueprint templates in a subfolder named after the blueprint to avoid clashes.</details>

### Async views on a sync framework

*deep · 4 min*

**In short:** Views and hooks may be `async def`. Flask wraps each one with `ensure_sync`, which uses asgiref to run the coroutine to completion on the worker thread; Flask itself stays a synchronous WSGI app.

Search app.py for `self.ensure_sync(` and you will find it around every user function Flask calls: before-request functions [`src/flask/app.py:1291`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1291), the view [`src/flask/app.py:902`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L902), after-request functions [`src/flask/app.py:1314`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1314), teardown functions [`src/flask/app.py:1356`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1356), error handlers [`src/flask/app.py:809`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L809) and context processors [`src/flask/app.py:530`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L530). Class-based views do the same around `dispatch_request` [`src/flask/views.py:110`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L110).

`ensure_sync` returns plain functions unchanged and wraps coroutine functions with `async_to_sync` [`src/flask/app.py:966-978`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L966-L978). That comes from asgiref, installed with the `async` extra; without it you get a `RuntimeError` telling you to install it [`src/flask/app.py:994-1001`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L994-L1001).

What you gain: `await` inside a view, for example to make several HTTP calls concurrently. What you do not gain: more concurrent requests. Each request still occupies a worker, and an async view is not faster than a sync one [`docs/async-await.rst:36-51`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/async-await.rst#L36-L51). Tasks spawned inside a view are cancelled when it returns [`docs/async-await.rst:54-60`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/async-await.rst#L54-L60).

Why not go fully async? The design notes say Flask must stay compatible with extensions and code written for WSGI, and that it is unclear whether one class can serve both ASGI and WSGI [`docs/design.rst:187-203`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/design.rst#L187-L203). Quart is the async-first framework that reuses Flask's sans-IO core.

Not everything is wrapped: URL value preprocessors are called directly [`src/flask/app.py:1283-1286`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1283-L1286), so they must be plain functions.

### Class-based views: View and MethodView

*deep · 4 min*

**In short:** `View.as_view()` turns a class into a view function; `MethodView` dispatches to methods named after HTTP verbs and fills in `methods` automatically.

Routing only knows functions, so class-based views are converted. `View.as_view(name, *args, **kwargs)` builds a function `view(**kwargs)` that, by default, creates a new instance per request and calls `dispatch_request` with the URL variables [`src/flask/views.py:104-116`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L104-L116). Set `init_every_request = False` and a single instance is created up front and shared by all requests; then you must not keep per-request data on `self` [`src/flask/views.py:66-76`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L66-L76).

The generated function is wrapped by every entry in the class's `decorators` list (decorators on the class itself would not apply) and gets the attributes the router reads: `view_class`, `methods` and `provide_automatic_options` [`src/flask/views.py:118-135`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L118-L135). `add_url_rule` uses `view_func.methods` when you pass no `methods` [`src/flask/sansio/app.py:621-622`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/sansio/app.py#L621-L622).

`MethodView` adds two things. `__init_subclass__` scans the class for methods named `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, `head`, `options` and `trace` and sets `methods` from them, merged with any base class's methods [`src/flask/views.py:165-180`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L165-L180). `dispatch_request` calls the method matching `request.method`, falling back from `HEAD` to `get` [`src/flask/views.py:182-191`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/views.py#L182-L191). A method the class does not define never reaches it, because routing answers 405 first: `methods` lists only what exists.

This is how REST-style resources are usually written: one class with `get` and `post` for a collection, another with `get`, `patch` and `delete` for an item, each registered with `add_url_rule(..., view_func=Cls.as_view('name'))`.

### Signals: observing without changing

*deep · 4 min*

**In short:** Flask sends ten Blinker signals at fixed points. They let extensions and tests observe requests, templates, flashes and context changes without changing behaviour.

All ten are created from one namespace in `signals.py` [`src/flask/signals.py:6-17`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/signals.py#L6-L17). Where each is sent:
- `request_started`: the start of `full_dispatch_request` [`src/flask/app.py:914`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L914).
- `request_finished`: after `process_response`, with the response [`src/flask/app.py:942-944`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L942-L944).
- `got_request_exception`: the start of `handle_exception` [`src/flask/app.py:840`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L840).
- `request_tearing_down`: the end of `do_teardown_request` [`src/flask/app.py:1358`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1358).
- `appcontext_tearing_down`: the end of `do_teardown_appcontext` [`src/flask/app.py:1384`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1384).
- `appcontext_pushed` and `appcontext_popped`: in `AppContext.push` and `pop` [`src/flask/ctx.py:251-272`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L251-L272).
- `before_render_template` and `template_rendered`: around rendering [`src/flask/templating.py:126-135`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/templating.py#L126-L135).
- `message_flashed`: in `flash()` [`src/flask/helpers.py:336-342`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/helpers.py#L336-L342).

The sender is always the app object, so a receiver connected with `sender=app` hears only that app. Every send passes `_async_wrapper=app.ensure_sync`, so an `async def` receiver runs like an async view.

Signals are for observing. A receiver's return value is ignored and it cannot stop the request; for that use hooks (`before_request` can return a response, `after_request` can replace it). Because `got_request_exception` is sent even when the error is about to be re-raised in debug mode, it is a good place for error reporting.

## How it flows

### The request pipeline in four layers

*core · 10 min*

**In short:** Every request runs the same pipeline in `wsgi_app`: push contexts and open the session, match the URL, run before-hooks, call the view, convert the result, run after-hooks and save the session, hand back the response, then tear down.

The step-through below follows the code line by line. Here is the shape to keep in your head: four nested layers.

**`wsgi_app`, the outer shell** [`src/flask/app.py:1506-1527`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1506-L1527). It creates the `RequestContext`, pushes it, calls `full_dispatch_request`, and turns any exception that escapes into a 500 with `handle_exception`. Its `finally` block always pops the context, which is why teardown functions run even after a crash.

**`RequestContext.push`** [`src/flask/ctx.py:367-394`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L367-L394) makes the globals work: app context, `_cv_request`, session, URL match. Matching never raises here; a failure is parked on `request.routing_exception`.

**`full_dispatch_request`** [`src/flask/app.py:904-920`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L904-L920) runs the `before_request` functions; if one returns a value, that is the response. Otherwise `dispatch_request` raises the parked routing error or calls the view. Any exception goes to error-handler lookup. Whatever produced a value (hook, view or handler) goes to `finalize_request`.

**`finalize_request`** [`src/flask/app.py:922-951`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L922-L951) calls `make_response`, then `process_response`: `after_this_request` callbacks, `after_request` functions, `save_session`. When it finalizes an error response it logs failures instead of raising, so a broken after-hook cannot hide the original error.

Order matters in a few places you will notice in practice:
- The session is opened before URL matching and saved after all after-hooks.
- If the view raises, no handler exists and propagation is on (testing or debug), `after_request` functions never run; `teardown_request` functions always do [`src/flask/app.py:1326-1358`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1326-L1358).
- Teardown runs after the response object is finished, so it cannot change the response.

The official docs list the same sequence as 27 numbered steps [`docs/lifecycle.rst:119-163`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/docs/lifecycle.rst#L119-L163); the code is shorter than the list.

**Flow: One HTTP request, from the WSGI server to your view and back** (trigger: A browser sends GET /hello to a server running the app)

1. **The server calls the app object** [`src/flask/app.py:1529-1536`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1529-L1536) `__call__` only forwards to `wsgi_app`. Middleware is meant to replace `app.wsgi_app`, not `app`, so you keep a reference to the real object [`src/flask/app.py:1483-1490`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1483-L1490).
2. **A RequestContext wraps the environ** [`src/flask/app.py:1506`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1506) The constructor builds `app.request_class(environ)` and binds the URL map to this request; a bad Host header or similar becomes `request.routing_exception` instead of raising here [`src/flask/ctx.py:316-325`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L316-L325).
3. **The URL adapter checks the host** [`src/flask/app.py:445-466`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L445-L466) `create_url_adapter` applies `TRUSTED_HOSTS`, reads the host, and decides how `SERVER_NAME` and subdomains are used before binding Werkzeug's `Map` to the environ.
4. **Push: app context first, then the request context** [`src/flask/ctx.py:367-378`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L367-L378) If no app context for this app is active, one is created and pushed, then the request context is stored in its ContextVar. From now on `current_app`, `g`, `request` and `session` work.
5. **The session is opened** [`src/flask/ctx.py:384-389`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L384-L389) The session interface loads the session from the request (by default from the signed cookie). If it returns `None`, a `NullSession` takes its place.
6. **The URL is matched** [`src/flask/ctx.py:357-365`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L357-L365) Matching happens after the session is open, so custom URL converters can use it. On success `request.url_rule` and `request.view_args` are set; a 404, 405 or redirect is stored in `routing_exception` for later.
7. **full_dispatch_request starts the pipeline** [`src/flask/app.py:904-920`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L904-L920) It marks `_got_first_request` (which locks setup methods), sends `request_started`, runs the before-hooks, calls the view if no hook answered, and routes any exception to `handle_user_exception`.
8. **Before-request hooks** [`src/flask/app.py:1271-1296`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1271-L1296) URL value preprocessors run first, then `before_request` functions: the app's (`None` key) first, then each blueprint from outermost to innermost. The first non-`None` return value becomes the response and the view is skipped.
9. **The view is called** [`src/flask/app.py:879-902`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L879-L902) A stored routing error is raised now. `OPTIONS` gets an automatic answer if the rule allows it. Otherwise the endpoint's function is looked up and called with the URL variables as keyword arguments.
10. **Exceptions find an error handler** [`src/flask/app.py:779-809`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L779-L809) HTTP exceptions go to `handle_http_exception`; others look for a registered handler and are re-raised if there is none. A handler's return value is treated like a view's.
11. **The return value becomes a Response** [`src/flask/app.py:922-951`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L922-L951) `finalize_request` calls `make_response` (strings, dicts, tuples...), then `process_response`, then sends `request_finished`.
12. **After-request hooks and session save** [`src/flask/app.py:1298-1324`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1298-L1324) `after_this_request` callbacks run first, then `after_request` functions in reverse registration order, innermost blueprint first. Finally the session is saved onto the response unless it is a null session.
13. **Unhandled errors become a 500** [`src/flask/app.py:811-862`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L811-L862) Back in `wsgi_app`, anything that escaped goes to `handle_exception`: it sends `got_request_exception`, re-raises in debug or testing mode, otherwise logs it and finalizes an `InternalServerError` response (through a 500 handler if one exists).
14. **The response is sent** [`src/flask/app.py:1518`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1518) A Werkzeug `Response` is itself a WSGI app: calling it starts the response with status and headers and returns the body iterable to the server.
15. **Teardown and context pop** [`src/flask/app.py:1519-1527`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1519-L1527) In a `finally`, the request context is popped with the error (if any): `teardown_request` functions run, the request is closed, and the app context it pushed is popped, which runs `teardown_appcontext` functions [`src/flask/ctx.py:396-431`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L396-L431).

> **Checkpoint:** A `teardown_request` function needs to add a header to the response. Will that work?
> - Yes, it receives the response object
> - No; teardown receives only the exception and runs after the response is finished, so use `after_request`
> - Only if it returns the response
> - Only in debug mode
>
> <details><summary>Answer</summary>No; teardown receives only the exception and runs after the response is finished, so use `after_request`. Teardown functions are called with `exc` and their return value is ignored [`src/flask/app.py:1353-1356`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1353-L1356); `after_request` functions receive and return the response [`src/flask/app.py:1316-1319`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/app.py#L1316-L1319).</details>

### Pushing and popping contexts

*standard · 7 min*

**In short:** Contexts are pushed and popped with ContextVar tokens, and only the outermost pop runs teardown. Knowing this lets you run Flask code in tests, scripts, threads and streamed responses.

The step-through shows a test pushing a request context by hand. Three rules come out of the code.

**A request context brings its own app context, unless one for the same app is already active.** `push` stores `(token, app_ctx)`, where `app_ctx` is `None` if an existing one was reused [`src/flask/ctx.py:370-378`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L370-L378), and `pop` only pops what it pushed [`src/flask/ctx.py:425-426`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L425-L426). So inside `with app.app_context():` requests share your `g`; outside, each request gets a new one.

**Teardown runs once, on the last pop.** Both classes keep a list of tokens. `RequestContext.pop` tears down only when one token is left [`src/flask/ctx.py:404-414`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L404-L414); `AppContext.pop` checks the same before calling `do_teardown_appcontext` [`src/flask/ctx.py:258-262`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L258-L262). That makes re-pushing safe: `stream_with_context` pushes the current request context again inside the generator, and `copy_current_request_context` pushes a copy in another greenlet.

**Popping out of order is an error.** Each pop compares the current value with `self` and raises `AssertionError("Popped wrong ... context")` [`src/flask/ctx.py:428-431`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/ctx.py#L428-L431). If you see it, something pushed a context and never popped it; Flask's own suite catches exactly this with `leak_detector`.

Recipes:
- Script or shell: `with app.app_context(): init_db()`. `flask shell` and `@app.cli.command` do this for you [`src/flask/cli.py:380-402`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/cli.py#L380-L402).
- Unit-testing code that reads `request`: `with app.test_request_context('/path?x=1', method='POST'):`.
- Inspecting `request` after a test-client call: `with client: client.get('/')` keeps the contexts alive until the block ends [`src/flask/testing.py:249-262`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/testing.py#L249-L262).
- Streaming: decorate the generator with `@stream_with_context` [`src/flask/helpers.py:62-136`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/helpers.py#L62-L136).

**Flow: How `request` and `g` become available, and how they go away** (trigger: A test runs `with app.test_request_context('/?q=1'):` and then reads `request.args['q']` and `g`)

1. **The proxies are created at import time** [`src/flask/globals.py:24-51`](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/85c5d93cbd049c4bd0679c36fd1ddcae8c37b642/src/flask/globals.py#L24-L51) `current_app` and `g` read attributes of whatever `AppContext` is in `_cv_app`; `request` and `session` read the `RequestContext` in `_cv_request`. Nothing is bound yet.
